topics.title: Thunderstorm structure and life cycle
lesson: A thunderstorm needs three ingredients: moisture, instability and a lifting mechanism. Wind shear decides how organized and long-lived it becomes.

lesson.h: Life cycle of an ordinary (single-cell) storm

list: Cumulus stage: updraft only. Towering cumulus grows. NOAA: a downdraft forms within 15 to 20 minutes of the cell starting, and the updraft weakens at 25 to 30 minutes.
Mature stage: updraft and downdraft both present. Heaviest rain, hail, lightning, gusts. The anvil forms at the tropopause.
Dissipating stage: downdraft dominates and cuts off the warm moist inflow. The storm collapses.

Single-cell: weak shear, short-lived, generally 30 to 45 minutes. A pulse storm is a single cell with more instability that can give brief downbursts, small to moderate hail and sometimes a weak tornado.

Multicell cluster: the most common type, with cells at different stages. Each cell lasts about 30 minutes but the cluster can last several hours. New cells form where lift persists (fronts, dry lines, outflow boundaries, higher terrain).

Squall line (multicell line): outflows merge into a continuous gust front, new cells form on the leading edge and the line moves forward. Straight-line wind damage is common and bow echoes can form. The line weakens if the gust front pulls ahead of it.
Supercell: a rotating updraft (mesocyclone) in strong shear. Long-lived. Textbook source of the most severe storms.
CAPE (convective available potential energy): a measure of instability. High CAPE supports strong updrafts and large hail.
Lightning comes from charge separation, mostly through collisions between graupel and ice crystals in the presence of supercooled water.
Thunder is the shock wave from the rapid heating of air along the lightning channel.
Definition: a local storm produced by a cumulonimbus, always accompanied by lightning and thunder, usually with strong gusts, heavy rain, and sometimes hail. Lightning may not be visible.

A thunderstorm is reported at the station when thunder is first heard, or overhead lightning is seen and noise might mask thunder. It is treated as ended when 15 minutes pass without activity. No intensity is assigned.
Lightning remarks: OCNL (less than 1 flash per minute), FRQ (1 to 6 per minute), CONS (more than 6 per minute); types LTGCG, LTGIC, LTGCC, or LTNG if undetermined; and direction from the station.

lesson.note: No lift, no storm. Look for fronts, sea breeze fronts, outflow boundaries or terrain.

terms: Convective available potential energy: positive buoyant energy available to a rising parcel.
Boundary left by cold downdraft air that can trigger new storms.

questions.q: Which three ingredients are needed for a thunderstorm?
c: Moisture, instability and a lifting mechanism
Cold air, strong winds and a front
Ice, high pressure and calm winds
questions.e: Without moisture, instability, or lift, deep convection does not occur.

questions.q: Which stage of an ordinary thunderstorm has both updrafts and downdrafts?
questions.e: The mature stage has the heaviest precipitation and a coexisting updraft and downdraft.

questions.q: What defines a supercell?
questions.e: Rotation within the updraft allows the storm to sustain itself for hours.

questions.q: What dominates the dissipating stage of a thunderstorm?
questions.e: Cold downdraft air spreads out and cuts off warm inflow.

questions.q: How does charge separation in thunderstorms mainly occur?
c: Collisions of graupel and ice crystals in the presence of supercooled water
Friction between falling raindrops and the ground below cloud base
Solar heating of the anvil, which splits positive and negative ions
Dust and sea salt colliding inside the updraft below the freezing level
questions.e: Riming and collisions in the mixed-phase region transfer charge.

questions.q: Which stage of a thunderstorm cell is dominated by an updraft?
questions.e: The cumulus stage has updraft only; downdrafts begin when precipitation falls.

questions.q: How long does an ordinary single-cell thunderstorm cell typically last?
questions.e: NOAA: single cells in weak shear are short-lived, generally 30 to 45 minutes.

questions.q: Supercell storms are distinguished by:
c: Weak updrafts only, with a short life of about five minutes
A short life, no rotation and very little precipitation
Absence of rain and an anvil that lacks any overshooting top
questions.e: Strong shear sustains a rotating updraft.

questions.q: CAPE measures:
c: The height of the cloud top above sea level
The amount of wind shear between the surface and 6 km
The friction between the wind and the earth's surface
questions.e: Convective available potential energy is the buoyant energy of a parcel.

questions.q: Which element is NOT needed for deep convection?
c: Moisture in the lower layers of the atmosphere
Instability, where the lapse rate exceeds the moist adiabat
A lifting mechanism such as a front or heated ground
questions.e: Deep convection needs moisture, instability and lift.

questions.q: The anvil of a cumulonimbus is formed when the updraft:
c: Reaches the stable tropopause and spreads out
Meets a warm front and is deflected sideways at low levels
Falls below the freezing level and begins to melt
Collapses entirely when the downdraft cuts it off
questions.e: Rising air cannot penetrate the stable stratosphere and spreads.

questions.q: Lightning is described as FRQ in a METAR remark when flashes occur at about:
questions.e: MANOBS 6.5.2.1: OCNL less than one flash per minute, FRQ one to six, CONS more than six.

questions.q: When does an observer record the end of a thunderstorm?
c: After 15 minutes with no thunderstorm activity
As soon as the rain stops
When the anvil leaves the sky
questions.e: MANOBS 6.4.2.2: when thunderstorm activity has not occurred in the last 15 minutes, it is recorded as having ended 15 minutes before.

sources: NOAA National Weather Service, Types of Thunderstorms (weather.gov/spotterguide/types): single cell, pulse, multicell cluster and line, durations
MANOBS 8th ed. Am. 3 (full PDF): 6.4 thunderstorm definition and reporting (thunder heard or overhead lightning; ends after 15 minutes)
MANOBS 8th ed. Am. 3 (full PDF): 6.4 and 6.5 (thunderstorm and lightning definitions and reporting), 13.2.17
unverified: Supercell and mesocyclone definitions, and shear requirements: the NOAA page does not give them.
CAPE, charge separation by graupel and ice crystals, thunder, anvil at the tropopause: standard meteorology, not checked against a Canadian publication.
Cumulus-stage duration was removed (no source found).

topics.title: Tornadoes and downbursts
lesson: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air in contact with both the ground and a cloud base. A funnel cloud has the same rotation but does not reach the ground. A waterspout is a tornado over water.

list: Most strong tornadoes come from supercells. Weaker ones form in squall lines and along boundaries (landspouts).

Canada rates tornadoes with the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale, introduced by ECCC on 1 April 2013 to replace the F-scale. Ratings come from damage (31 damage indicators, from houses to trees), not from measured wind.
ECCC wind ranges (rounded to 5 km/h): EF0 90 to 130. EF1 135 to 175. EF2 180 to 220. EF3 225 to 265. EF4 270 to 310. EF5 315 or more.

lesson: A downburst is a strong downdraft from a thunderstorm that hits the ground and spreads outward in a damaging burst of wind.

list: Microburst: a small downburst, textbook size under about 4 km across and short-lived. NOAA notes pulse storms give brief downbursts, usually under 70 mph (about 110 km/h).
Macroburst: larger than a microburst, lasts longer.
Wet microburst: with heavy rain. Dry microburst: little or no rain reaches the ground, often with high-based storms.

lesson: On approach, an aircraft meets a strong headwind first (airspeed increases), then strong sink, then a tailwind (airspeed falls rapidly). This sequence has caused major accidents. Avoid thunderstorms by a wide margin, including near the storm's outflow.

list: MANOBS definitions: a tornado is a rotating column of air extending from the base of a cumuliform cloud (usually cumulonimbus), often visible as a condensation funnel in contact with the ground and/or a circulating dust or debris cloud. A waterspout is a tornado over water, normally small and weak, below cumulonimbus or towering cumulus. A cold-air funnel is a funnel cloud, rarely a small weak tornado, that can develop from a small shower or thunderstorm when the air aloft is unusually cold.

Coding: +FC for a tornado (over land) or waterspout (over water) within sight; FC for a funnel cloud. A tornado or waterspout is not reported if the vortex does not reach the ground, or the observer is unsure it does; then FC is reported. TORNADO, FUNNEL CLOUD or WATERSPOUT is spelled out in the remarks. No intensity is given.

lesson.note: Damage to the ground tells you the rating. The rating is assigned after the event, not during it.

terms: Rotating cloud extending from a cumuliform base that does not reach the ground.
Enhanced Fujita scale: damage-based rating of tornado intensity. ECCC ranges run from EF0 (90 to 130 km/h) to EF5 (315 km/h or more).
Localized downburst less than 4 km across.

questions.q: Which scale does Canada use to rate tornadoes?
questions.e: EF ratings are assigned from observed damage.

questions.q: What is the size of a microburst?
questions.e: Microbursts are less than 4 km in extent; larger ones are macrobursts.

questions.q: What does an aircraft on approach experience when it flies through a microburst?
c: Headwind increase, then sink, then strong tailwind
Tailwind increase, then calm air, then a strong headwind
A steady crosswind with no change in airspeed or sink rate
A smooth decrease in airspeed with a gradual increase in climb rate
questions.e: Airspeed first rises, then falls sharply as the aircraft exits into the tailwind.

questions.q: What is the difference between a tornado and a funnel cloud?
c: A tornado reaches the ground; a funnel cloud does not
A funnel cloud reaches the ground; a tornado stays aloft
A tornado forms only over water and a funnel cloud only on land
A funnel cloud always has stronger surface winds than a tornado
questions.e: A tornado is in contact with the ground; a funnel cloud is not.

questions.q: How is a tornado's EF rating determined?
questions.e: EF ratings use damage indicators to estimate the wind.

questions.q: Tornado intensity in Canada is rated with the:
questions.e: Damage-based EF scale is used in Canada.

questions.q: A downburst is:
c: A strong downdraft that spreads outward at the surface
A rising current of warm air that forms over heated ground
A tornado that has lifted off the ground but still rotates
A funnel cloud that never reaches the surface or does damage
questions.e: Downbursts produce straight-line wind damage.

questions.q: A microburst has a damage path of:
questions.e: Microbursts are less than 4 km across; macrobursts exceed it.

questions.q: Why are microbursts dangerous to aircraft on approach?
c: Sudden shift from headwind to tailwind reduces lift
Sudden shift from tailwind to headwind adds lift and speed
Heavy rain reduces visibility only, with no effect on lift
Icing on the wings from supercooled drops at low level
questions.e: A rapid headwind loss near the ground can cause a loss of performance.

questions.q: A hook echo on radar suggests:
c: A gentle rain shower with light winds and no organized structure
A snow squall passing the station with strong gusts
Ground clutter from nearby hills returning a stable echo
questions.e: Hook shapes mark the mesocyclone's region.

questions.q: The most reliable way to confirm a tornado is:
questions.e: Radar suggests; spotters and damage surveys confirm.

questions.q: Which wind range does ECCC give for an EF2 tornado?
An observer sees a funnel but is not sure it reaches the ground. What is reported?
questions.e: MANOBS 6.3.2 item 4: a tornado or waterspout is not reported when the observer is not sure the vortex reaches the ground; funnel cloud (FC) and its direction are reported.

questions.q: In a METAR, which code reports a tornado within sight?
questions.e: MANOBS 6.3.2: +FC for a tornado or waterspout, FC for a funnel cloud.

sources: ECCC, Enhanced Fujita scale for wind damage (canada.ca): wind ranges, 31 damage indicators, introduced 1 April 2013
ECCC Weather Impact Guides, Tornadoes: effects at moderate, high and extreme levels
NOAA National Weather Service, Types of Thunderstorms: pulse-storm downbursts, bow echo tornadoes weaker than supercell tornadoes
MANOBS 8th ed. Am. 3 (full PDF): 6.3 tornado, waterspout and funnel cloud definitions
MANOBS 8th ed. Am. 3 (full PDF): 6.3 (tornado, waterspout, funnel cloud definitions and coding), 13.2.5 and 13.2.18 to 13.2.19
unverified: Microburst size (under 4 km) and the headwind, sink, tailwind sequence: standard teaching, not checked against a Canadian publication. Duration and the 150 km/h figure were removed.
Hook echo and radar signatures: not checked.

topics.title: Winter storms and freezing precipitation
lesson: Atlantic Canada gets winter storms from lows tracking up the east coast (nor'easters), from lows moving in from the Great Lakes, and from systems that redevelop near Cape Hatteras.

list: Heavy snow: reduces visibility and blocks roads.

Blizzard: strong wind with snow or blowing snow and very low visibility. ECCC now covers blizzards in its Visibility Impact Guide. The old numeric criteria (wind 40 km/h or more, visibility 400 m or less, 4 hours) are no longer listed on the ECCC page and are not confirmed here.

Freezing rain: supercooled rain freezes on contact. ECCC's Ice guide scales it from ice on power lines and bridges with some outages (moderate), to damaged lines and widespread outages (high), to collapsed poles and towers with long outages (extreme). See precipitation processes.
Ice pellets: stinging pellets, slippery surfaces.
Snow squalls: sudden, short bursts of intense snow with strong wind and whiteout, typically near a front or lake.

Wind chill (ECCC): -28 to -39, exposed skin can freeze in 10 to 30 minutes. -40 to -47, 5 to 10 minutes. -48 to -54, 2 to 5 minutes. -55 or colder, under 2 minutes. In sustained wind over 50 km/h frostbite can come faster.

lesson: Precipitation type depends on the temperature profile through the whole column. A thin warm layer near the surface can turn snow into rain. A thin cold layer at the surface under a warm layer aloft produces freezing rain. Surface temperatures near 0 C often mean a messy mix.

A coastal low that intensifies off the US east coast and tracks toward the Maritimes, often with heavy snow, strong northeast winds, coastal flooding, and sometimes rain along the shore. Small track changes shift the rain-snow line by tens of kilometres.

lesson.note: Marginal temperatures make the forecast hardest. Always check the 850 hPa temperature and the surface temperature together.

terms: Strong wind with snow or blowing snow and very low visibility for a sustained period. ECCC covers it in the Visibility Impact Guide.
Coastal storm with strong northeast winds.
Index of the cooling effect of wind on exposed skin. ECCC hazard levels run from low (0 to -9) to extreme (-55 or colder).

questions.q: In ECCC's Impact Guides, which hazard guide covers blizzards?
c: Visibility (including blizzards, blowing snow, dust, fog)
questions.e: ECCC lists blizzards under Visibility. There is no separate blizzard guide.

questions.q: Which temperature profile is typical for freezing rain?
c: Above 0 C aloft, below 0 C near the surface
Below 0 C aloft, above 0 C at the surface
questions.e: Snow melts in the warm layer, then rain supercools in the shallow cold layer.

questions.q: What is a nor'easter?
c: A coastal storm with strong northeast winds
A tropical storm approaching from the south in summer
A thunderstorm complex moving in from the northeast
A sea breeze that blows from the northeast each afternoon
questions.e: Nor'easters track along the east coast and bring heavy snow or rain with strong NE winds.

questions.q: What is a snow squall?
c: A brief burst of intense snow with strong wind and low visibility
A long period of light, steady snow with calm winds and good visibility
A layer of ice that coats surfaces after freezing drizzle overnight
A thin fog that forms over snow-covered ground on clear nights
questions.e: Squalls can cause whiteouts and rapid road deterioration.

questions.q: Why are marginal surface temperatures near 0 C a forecast challenge?
c: Small changes shift precipitation between snow, rain and freezing rain
Precipitation cannot form at all when the surface temperature is near 0 C
Models cannot represent temperatures when they are close to the freezing mark
Snow always melts instantly, so no frozen precipitation can reach the ground
questions.e: Tiny temperature differences change the precipitation type and impacts.

questions.q: Freezing rain differs from ice pellets because freezing rain:
c: Freezes on impact with the surface
questions.e: Ice pellets are already frozen when they arrive.

questions.q: A blizzard involves:
c: Strong wind, blowing snow and low visibility for hours
Light snow and calm winds persisting for several hours
Rain falling on frozen ground and freezing on contact
Freezing fog that reduces visibility but brings no wind
questions.e: A blizzard combines strong wind, blowing snow and very low visibility for a sustained time. ECCC handles it under the Visibility Impact Guide.

questions.q: Lake-effect snow occurs when:
c: Cold air crosses warmer open water
Warm air crosses colder water or ice and forms fog
Winds are calm and the sky is clear over the lake
A front stalls over the lake with a deep layer of warm air
questions.e: Heat and moisture from the lake destabilize the air.

questions.q: What temperature profile gives ice pellets?
c: Warm layer aloft and a deep sub-zero layer below
Cold air through the whole depth from cloud top to the ground
Warm air through the whole depth from cloud base to the ground
An isothermal layer at 0 C from the surface to 3 km
questions.e: Raindrops refreeze in a deep cold layer.

questions.q: Snow squalls are:
c: Intense, short-lived snowfall with strong gusts
Steady snow for most of a day with very light winds
Large hail falling from a thunderstorm in winter
Drizzle that freezes on contact and builds a glaze
questions.e: They cut visibility quickly.

questions.q: What worsens ice accretion on power lines in freezing rain?
questions.e: Ice weight plus wind stress can bring lines and trees down.

questions.q: At a wind chill of -45, how fast can exposed skin freeze (ECCC)?
questions.e: ECCC: -40 to -47 gives 5 to 10 minutes; -28 to -39 gives 10 to 30; -48 to -54 gives 2 to 5; -55 or colder under 2.

sources: ECCC, Wind chill and the Wind Chill Index (canada.ca): hazard levels and frostbite times
ECCC Weather Impact Guides: Visibility (including blizzards), Ice (freezing rain, freezing drizzle, flash freeze), Snow squall, Winter storm sections
ECCC, Criteria for public weather alerts: notice that the criteria were replaced by Impact Guides (modified 2025-11-26)
unverified: Blizzard numbers (40 km/h, 400 m, 4 hours): not on any current ECCC page that could be read, so treated as unconfirmed. Questions use the Impact Guide wording instead.
Snow squall, nor'easter, lake-effect snow, and the temperature profiles for freezing rain and ice pellets: standard meteorology, not checked against a Canadian publication.
Wind chill formula: not given on the ECCC page.

topics.title: Turbulence (CAT, mechanical, mountain wave)
lesson: Turbulence is irregular air motion that causes bumpy flight. Intensity is described as light, moderate, severe or extreme.

list: Convective (thermal): rising thermals on sunny days over land, and in and near cumulus. Worst in the afternoon.
Mechanical: wind flowing over obstacles such as buildings, trees and hills. Worst at low levels in strong winds, with gusty approach and takeoff.

Mountain wave: stable air flowing across a ridge produces waves downwind. The AIM (AIR 1.5.6) says waves typically form when winds exceed about 50 kt and cross the range within 30 degrees of perpendicular, extending about 100 NM downwind. Lenticular clouds may mark a wave, but the AIM says there may be no lenticular clouds with a mountain wave (AIR 2.10). Mountain waves have occurred over the Appalachians (ridge about 4,500 ft ASL), not only the Rockies. Combined with non-standard temperature, a wave can make the altimeter overread by as much as 3,000 ft (AIR 1.5.8). Downdrafts are strongest near summit height, up to about 5,000 ft/min on the lee of high ranges, and flight in the wave can feel smooth (AIR 1.5.7).

Clear-air turbulence (CAT): in the TC AIM, turbulence normally above 15,000 ft ASL that is not associated with cumuliform cloud. The AIM rules of thumb (AIR 2.10, westerly jet streams): jet streams stronger than 110 kt at the core have significant turbulence near them in the sloping tropopause above the core, in the jet stream front below the core, and on the low-pressure side of the core.

Wake turbulence: vortices from the wingtips of heavy aircraft. Strongest when the aircraft is heavy, clean and slow, with little dissipation in the first 2 minutes. Generated from rotation to nosewheel touchdown (AIR 2.9).

lesson: The Richardson number compares stability to wind shear. When it falls below the textbook critical value of about 0.25, shear overcomes stability and Kelvin-Helmholtz waves form. Strong shear with weak stability produces CAT.

list: Thunderstorms: severe turbulence can extend up to 20 NM from a severe storm and beneath it even with little visible sign. The AIM advises avoiding severe storms by at least 20 NM, and calls storms with tops at 35,000 ft or higher severe (AIR 2.7).
CAT is hard to see. Forecast it from jet stream, shear, and pilot reports.
Change altitude if turbulence persists.

lesson.note: Lenticular clouds can mark a mountain wave, but a wave can occur with no lenticular cloud. Smooth air in a wave can hide strong downdrafts.

list: Light (LGT): momentary, slight erratic changes in altitude and/or attitude (pitch, roll, yaw).
Moderate (MOD): similar to light but greater. Altitude/attitude changes occur, but the aircraft stays in positive control at all times. Usually changes indicated airspeed.
Severe (SEV): large, abrupt changes in altitude/attitude. Usually large variations in indicated airspeed. The aircraft may be momentarily out of control.
Light: slight, momentary erratic changes in altitude or attitude, or slight rhythmic bumpiness reported as 'light chop'.

Moderate: greater than light; altitude or attitude changes occur but the aircraft stays in positive control. Usually airspeed variations. Sharp bumps without major altitude change are 'moderate chop'.
Severe: large abrupt changes in altitude or attitude and large airspeed variations; the aircraft may be momentarily out of control.
Extreme is listed as a reportable intensity (MET 2.2.1) but not defined in Table 2.2.
Frequency: occasional is less than one third of the time, intermittent one third to two thirds, continuous more than two thirds.
High-level turbulence (normally above 15,000 ft ASL) not associated with cumuliform cloud is reported as CAT.
Weather radar cannot detect turbulence.
A report should include location, UTC time, intensity, in or near cloud, altitude, aircraft type, and duration where applicable.
The 2026 AIM GFA text labels turbulence causes MECH, L LVL WS, LEE WV, L LVL JET and CAT. MANAIR 2024 lists the lee wave type as MTW.
CAT shear is more intense above and to the lee of mountain ranges. Expect CAT when the flight path crosses a strong jet stream near mountains.
On 250 mb charts, 30 kt isotachs closer than 90 NM indicate enough horizontal shear for CAT. This is normally on the north (low-pressure) side of the jet axis, but can be on the south side.

Vertical shear above 5 kt per 1,000 ft makes turbulence likely. If the 5 C isotherms on an upper-air chart are closer than 2 degrees of latitude (120 NM), vertical shear is usually enough for turbulence.
Curving jet streams, especially around a deep trough, are more apt to have turbulent edges. Wind-shift areas with troughs are frequently turbulent, and ridge lines may also have rough air.

Escape: for direct tailwinds or headwinds, change flight level or course. A turn to the south in the Northern Hemisphere places the aircraft in a more favourable area. In a crosswind, climb if temperature is rising and descend if falling. For an abrupt wind shift at a sharp trough, cross the trough rather than fly parallel to it.
Where significant CAT is reported or forecast, adjust to turbulence penetration speed before the first ripple.
Two counter-rotating vortices from the wingtips, a by-product of lift. Strength depends on wing shape, weight and speed; greatest when heavy, clean and slow.
Vortices begin to descend immediately at 400 to 500 ft per minute for large heavy aircraft, and descend less than 1,000 ft in total in 2 minutes.
Vortices spread out at about 5 kt. A light wind of 3 to 7 kt can keep the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone.
Vortex cores can produce a roll rate of 80 degrees per second and a downdraft of 1,500 ft per minute.
ATC uses the words CAUTION - WAKE TURBULENCE.
GFA types of turbulence: CAT, MECH (mechanical), MTW (lee waves), L LVL JET and L LVL WS.
The GFA depicts only moderate or severe NON-CONVECTIVE turbulence. Light turbulence goes in the comments box.
Turbulence layers are written as a fraction: top over base, in hundreds of feet ASL.
A low-level jet (L LVL JET) is included in the GFA at 50 kt or more. It may be included at 35 to 45 kt if the forecaster expects significant turbulence or shear. Rounded to the nearest 5 kt.

SIGMET: SEV TURB only. AIRMET: MOD TURB only. Both refer only to low-level turbulence with strong surface winds, rotor streaming, and high-level CAT (SIGMET) or CAT near jet streams (AIRMET). Turbulence is never used for convective clouds.
The GFA legend states: CB, TCU and ACC imply significant turbulence and icing.

terms: Clear-air turbulence. In the TC AIM: above 15,000 ft ASL and not associated with cumuliform cloud.
Smooth lens-shaped cloud that marks the crest of a mountain wave.
Ratio of stability to shear. Turbulence develops when it falls below about 0.25.
Low-level jet. In the GFA when 50 kt or more (35 to 45 kt at the forecaster's judgment).

questions.q: Clear-air turbulence is usually associated with:
c: Strong wind shear near jet streams and the tropopause
Low-level fog and haze trapped beneath a surface inversion
Heated ground over desert regions on hot summer afternoons
Warm fronts moving slowly across flat terrain at night
questions.e: CAT develops in cloud-free air where wind shear is strong.

questions.q: What does a lenticular cloud indicate?
questions.e: Lenticulars form at wave crests in stable air flowing over mountains.

questions.q: What does a Richardson number below about 0.25 indicate?
c: Shear instability that can generate turbulence
Very stable air in which turbulence cannot develop
Fog and low stratus forming beneath a surface inversion
Dry adiabatic conditions with no wind shear in the layer
questions.e: Shear dominates over stability, so waves break into turbulence.

questions.q: Which turbulence type is typically worst on hot afternoons over land?
questions.e: Strong surface heating produces vigorous thermals.

questions.q: What conditions favour a mountain wave?
c: Strong wind across a ridge, increasing with height, with a stable layer
Light winds blowing parallel to the ridge with a deep unstable layer above it
Calm wind at ridge height and strong thermal heating on the lee slope
Strong winds that decrease with height above a ridge in very unstable air
questions.e: Stable flow across a barrier sets up downwind waves.

questions.q: Clear-air turbulence is most often associated with:
questions.e: Strong shear near jets causes CAT.

questions.q: Mountain wave turbulence is most severe:
c: On the lee side, downstream of the ridge
On the windward side, upstream of the ridge, close to the surface
Over open water far from any terrain and any ridge
Over flat terrain beneath a strong subsidence inversion
questions.e: Lee waves and rotors form downwind.

questions.q: Mechanical turbulence is caused by:
c: Wind flowing over rough terrain or obstacles
Convection from strongly heated ground in the afternoon
Jet stream shear at the tropopause in clear air
Solar radiation heating the surface in bright sunshine
questions.e: Obstacles disturb airflow near the surface.

questions.q: Thermal turbulence is strongest:
c: On sunny afternoons over heated land
At night over water, when winds are calm and the air is stable
In stable air beneath a strong, low-level inversion
Inside a surface inversion on a clear, calm morning
questions.e: Daytime heating drives thermals.

questions.q: Moderate turbulence can cause:
c: Changes in altitude or attitude and strain against belts
No effect on the aircraft or its occupants at all
Only a slight bump that is barely noticeable to crew
Structural failure of the airframe in nearly every case
questions.e: Moderate turbulence makes walking difficult and unsecured items shift.

questions.q: A rotor cloud is associated with:
c: Calm air and unlimited visibility in the lee of the ridge
Icing only, with no turbulence or vertical motion
Dense fog trapped in the valley below the ridge crest
questions.e: Rotor circulation beneath lee waves is violent.

questions.q: Which turbulence intensity can leave the aircraft momentarily out of control (MANAIR)?
questions.e: MANAIR 4.9.2.2: severe turbulence causes large abrupt changes and the aircraft may be momentarily out of control.

questions.q: In MANAIR, how is moderate turbulence distinguished from light?
c: Greater intensity; altitude/attitude changes occur but the aircraft remains in positive control, and airspeed usually changes
Any change in indicated airspeed, which also occurs in light turbulence
It is judged only by the type of aircraft affected
Turbulence lasting more than one hour continuously
questions.e: MANAIR 4.9.2.2 definition of MOD.

questions.q: Where is light turbulence given on the GFA?
questions.e: MANAIR 4.9.2.2: only MOD and SEV are depicted; light goes in the comments box.

questions.q: A low-level jet is shown in the GFA when it reaches at least:
c: 50 kt (35 to 45 kt if significant turbulence or shear is expected)
25 kt, since any wind maximum is plotted
75 kt, the criterion for jet streams
questions.e: MANAIR 4.9.2.2.

questions.q: Which turbulence intensity does a SIGMET cover?
questions.e: MANAIR 5.8.3.2: TURB, only SEV. AIRMETs cover only MOD.

questions.q: Turbulence in the GFA, SIGMET or AIRMET sense is NOT used for:
c: Low-level turbulence with strong surface winds
questions.e: MANAIR D.5 and E.5 notes: turbulence shall not be used in connection with convective clouds.

questions.q: Which is NOT a GFA turbulence type?
questions.e: MANAIR 4.9.2.2 lists CAT, MECH, MTW, L LVL JET and L LVL WS.

questions.q: In the AIM, 'intermittent' turbulence means:
c: One third to two thirds of the time
Less than one third of the time
More than two thirds of the time
questions.e: AIM MET 2.2.2: occasional is less than 1/3, intermittent is 1/3 to 2/3, continuous is more than 2/3.

questions.q: How does the AIM treat 'moderate chop'?
c: Sharp bumps without major altitude change
questions.e: AIM MET 2.2.2. Slight rhythmic bumpiness is light chop.

questions.q: Can weather radar detect turbulence?
questions.e: AIM MET 1.3.9.1: these radars cannot detect turbulence.

questions.q: Roughly how far from a severe thunderstorm can severe turbulence extend, per the AIM?

topics.title: Wind shear and low-level jets
lesson: Wind shear is a change in wind speed or direction over a short distance. The TC AIM sets no height limit for wind shear. Shear near the ground (low-level wind shear, LLWS) is the major hazard on approach and takeoff.

list: Thunderstorm outflow and microbursts.
Fronts, especially fast-moving cold fronts and warm fronts at low level.
Strong surface inversions: calm at the surface under strong wind just above, typical on clear nights.
Sea breeze fronts.
Terrain and obstacles close to the runway.

lesson: After sunset the surface layer decouples from the air above because of a nocturnal inversion. Friction no longer holds back the winds a few hundred metres up, and they accelerate. A wind maximum forms a few hundred metres above the ground, strongest in the early morning. It is common over flat land such as the Great Plains and can also occur near coasts.

On approach, an aircraft may fly from a strong wind at 500 ft to calm air at the surface. Airspeed drops rapidly and the aircraft sinks below the glide path. Pilots add speed margin and are briefed on reported LLWS.

lesson.note: Light winds at the surface on a clear night do not mean light winds above. Check the winds aloft along the approach path.

lesson: In a TAF, non-convective low-level wind shear within 1,500 ft AGL is coded as a WS group. It is included when the forecaster has strong evidence of significant shear that could adversely affect aircraft. These guidelines are at the forecaster's discretion:

list: Vector magnitude exceeding 25 kt within 500 ft AGL.
Vector magnitude exceeding 40 kt within 1,000 ft AGL.
Vector magnitude exceeding 50 kt within 1,500 ft AGL.
A pilot report of loss or gain of indicated airspeed of 20 kt or more within 1,500 ft AGL.
Intense downdrafts, typically from thunderstorms, create wind shear that is hazardous on approach, landing and takeoff (MET 2.3).
Ground instruments do not measure wind shear at Canadian aerodromes, so it is usually identified from pilot reports (MET 2.3).

Microburst (AIR 2.8): wind shear may be severe within 1,000 ft AGL, especially on approach and takeoff. About 1 NM across at 2,000 ft AGL, surface spread about 2 to 2.5 NM. Vertical winds up to 6,000 ft/min and surface horizontal winds up to 45 kt (90 kt shear). Usually accompanied by heavy rain; in drier air, rain may evaporate before reaching the ground (virga). Life cycle seldom longer than 15 minutes, peak winds 2 to 4 minutes; multiple microbursts are common. Recovery may need full power and a pitch attitude consistent with maximum angle of attack. On takeoff an aircraft may meet a headwind, then a downdraft, then a tailwind.
Format: WSh(3 digits)/dddffKT, for example WS015/24045KT. Height is in hundreds of feet AGL; the wind is at that height. No gusts in this group.
Wind shear cannot be satisfactorily observed from the ground. Aircraft reports and radiosondes are the only available evidence.
WS is not part of the international TAF code. It is used in North American TAFs.
A SIGMET for L LVL WS is issued only for severe shear.
The GFA legend states: CB implies L LVL WS.

terms: Low-level wind shear: wind shear close to the ground, where it affects takeoff and landing. The AIM sets no height limit for wind shear.
Temperature inversion that forms near the ground at night.
Layer of strong winds a few hundred metres above the surface.
TAF group for non-convective low-level wind shear within 1,500 ft AGL: WShhh/dddffKT.

questions.q: What height limit does the TC AIM put on wind shear?
c: None; wind shear can occur at any height
Only the lowest 2,000 ft above the ground
Only within 500 ft of the runway
questions.e: AIM MET 2.3 does not limit wind shear to a height band. Shear near the ground matters most for takeoff and landing.

questions.q: Why does a nocturnal low-level jet form?
c: A surface inversion decouples the surface from the air above, so winds aloft accelerate
Surface friction increases at night and pushes extra wind into the layer above
Heat from the sun in the evening accelerates the air a few hundred metres up
Cold fronts always pass during the night and create a jet along the boundary
questions.e: Reduced friction above the nocturnal inversion allows winds to speed up.

questions.q: What is a typical cause of wind shear near airports?
questions.e: Outflow and microbursts create sudden speed and direction changes.

questions.q: A clear, calm night with a strong inversion and strong winds above can produce:
questions.e: Light surface wind beneath strong wind aloft gives strong shear in a shallow layer.

questions.q: When does the nocturnal low-level jet usually peak?
questions.e: The jet strengthens during the night and often peaks near dawn.

questions.q: Low-level wind shear is the change of wind over:
c: A short distance in the vertical or horizontal near the ground
Hundreds of kilometres in the horizontal across a frontal zone
The whole depth of the troposphere from surface to tropopause
A time interval of several days at a fixed location
questions.e: Wind shear is a change in wind speed and/or direction over a short distance.

questions.q: A nocturnal low-level jet usually forms:
c: At noon, when the surface is heated and mixing is strongest
Over the ocean only, well away from any coast
In the stratosphere above the tropopause in winter
questions.e: Decoupled flow above the inversion accelerates.

questions.q: Wind shear on approach from tailwind to headwind causes:
c: An increase in airspeed and lift
A decrease in airspeed and a loss of lift on the approach
No change at all in airspeed, lift or sink rate
A drop in lift only, with airspeed unchanged
questions.e: A gain in headwind raises airspeed relative to the air.

questions.q: Which weather commonly causes LLWS?
c: Light haze and clear skies with no wind at the surface
Clear, calm days with a deep well-mixed boundary layer
Stratus with no wind and a uniform temperature profile
questions.e: Frontal passages, gust fronts and inversions change wind sharply.

questions.q: The unit of wind shear is often expressed as:
questions.e: Shear is wind change over distance.

questions.q: A pilot reports airspeed gain of 20 kt on short final. This indicates:
c: A possible shear to a headwind
A possible shear to a tailwind that reduces airspeed
Icing on the pitot tube giving a falsely high reading
A compass error caused by a magnetic disturbance
questions.e: Increased airspeed at constant power suggests increasing headwind.

questions.q: In a TAF, the WS group refers to non-convective wind shear within:
questions.e: MANAIR 2.6.9.

questions.q: Which is a MANAIR guideline for significant low-level wind shear?
c: Vector magnitude over 40 kt within 1,000 ft AGL
Vector magnitude over 10 kt within 1,500 ft AGL
A 5 kt airspeed change reported by a pilot
questions.e: MANAIR 2.6.9 lists >25 kt/500 ft, >40 kt/1,000 ft, >50 kt/1,500 ft, and a PIREP of 20 kt IAS loss or gain within 1,500 ft.

questions.q: How would wind shear at 1,500 ft AGL with a 240 degree, 45 kt wind be coded in a TAF?
questions.e: Format WShhh/dddffKT: height in hundreds of feet AGL, then direction and speed (MANAIR 2.6.9).

There are no wind observations at airports
TAFs only cover convective weather, so shear is excluded
Shear never occurs below 1,500 ft AGL

questions.e: MANAIR 5.8.3.2: L LVL WS only SEV.

questions.q: The GFA legend statement 'CB IMPLIES L LVL WS' means:
c: Cumulonimbus clouds imply low-level wind shear
Cloud base is lowered by wind shear
questions.e: MANAIR 4.8 (legend box standard phrases).

questions.q: How is wind shear usually identified at Canadian aerodromes, per the AIM?
c: Pilot reports, since ground instruments do not measure it
Ground wind shear sensors at every aerodrome
questions.e: AIM MET 2.3.

questions.q: How long do peak microburst winds usually last, per the AIM?
questions.e: AIM AIR 2.8, summarised read: usually 15 minutes or less overall.

questions.q: On a takeoff through a microburst, which sequence is typical, per the AIM?
c: Increasing headwind, then downdraft, then tailwind
questions.e: AIM AIR 2.8, Figure 2.8.

topics.title: Weather alerts and Impact Guides (ECCC)
lesson: ECCC replaced its former public weather alert criteria with Impact Guides. The Canada.ca criteria page now only points to them (page modified 2025-11-26). The old numbers for hail, gusts and rain no longer apply, so do not memorize them.

list: 14 hazard guides: coastal flooding and storm surge, cold, frost, heat, hurricanes and tropical storms, ice, rain, snow, snow squall, thunderstorms, tornadoes, visibility, wind, winter storm.
Blizzards sit under Visibility. Freezing rain sits under Ice.
Most hazards have three impact levels: moderate, high, extreme. Frost has only a moderate level. They describe effects on daily life, travel, utilities, land and structures, health and recovery.
The guides describe effects, not numeric thresholds.

lesson.h: How the alert colour is chosen

lesson: ECCC uses an Alert Colour Matrix: forecast confidence (low, moderate, high, very high) on one axis and weather impact (low, moderate, high, extreme) on the other. Where they meet gives the colour. Confidence comes from current observations, weather prediction models and forecaster expertise; the forecaster decides the level.

list: Very high confidence: moderate impact is yellow, high is orange, extreme is red.
High confidence: moderate impact is yellow, high and extreme are orange.
Moderate confidence: moderate impact is no alert, high is yellow, extreme is orange.
Low confidence: moderate impact is no alert, high and extreme are yellow.
Low impact: no alert at any confidence. ECCC may issue a MetNote or special weather statement instead.
Example from ECCC: with very high confidence in a thunderstorm, moderate impact gives yellow, high gives orange, extreme gives red.
Alerts are issued for only three impact levels: moderate, high and extreme.
Impact levels describe effects on travel delays, utilities disruption, damage to property, danger to health and time for society to recover.
Not every impact listed in a guide must occur for that level to apply.
Impacts listed at lower levels also apply at higher levels, even if not repeated.
The guides give primary impacts for the average person in the forecast area. They exclude secondary impacts such as business or school closures.
The same weather can have different impacts depending on location, existing conditions (such as snow already on the ground), timing and vulnerability of the area or people.
Thunderstorms: moderate is difficult driving and damage to roofs, fences and trees. Extreme is destroyed buildings and many trees.
Tornadoes: high is significant widespread tree damage. Extreme is destroyed homes and collapsed utility towers.
Ice: extreme is collapsed poles and towers with long, widespread outages.
Wind: high is some roof damage and small to medium trees snapped. Extreme is structural damage to homes and high-sided vehicles tipped or flipped.
Rain: high is widespread overland flooding with some washouts and landslides. Extreme is major roads, highways or bridges washed out and dams, dikes or pumps compromised.
Snow: high is dangerous travel and roofs at increased risk of collapse. Extreme is travel extremely unsafe or impossible and residents snowed in.
Winter storm: high is widespread road closures with vehicles and passengers stranded. Extreme is stranding for long periods and prolonged, widespread outages.

Hurricanes and tropical storms: high is major damage to buildings and widespread utility outages. Extreme is widespread building destruction and risk of life-threatening injury. The guide defines a tropical storm as 63 to 117 km/h winds and a hurricane as 118 km/h or more.

Coastal flooding and storm surge: moderate is some overland and basement flooding and shoreline erosion in sensitive areas. Extreme is travel routes impassable, widespread flooding and dikes or pumping infrastructure compromised.
Cold: moderate is risk of frostnip, frostbite or hypothermia without protection and pipes freezing or bursting. Extreme is a severe risk of cold injury and travel or outdoor activity not safe.
Heat: moderate is increased risk of illness or death and brownouts. Extreme is an extreme risk of illness or death and excess demand on utilities.
Frost: moderate only, widespread damage to plants or crops.
Snow squall: high is dangerous travel with stranded vehicles and roofs at risk of collapse. Extreme is very dangerous or impassable routes and long-stranded vehicles.
ECCC states the three types of alerts are warnings, advisories and watches. Each appears on a yellow, orange or red banner, which moves yellow to orange to red as potential risk increases.
Yellow: hazardous weather may cause damage, disruption or health impacts. Impacts are moderate, localized and/or short-term. Yellow is the most common.
Orange: severe weather is likely to cause significant damage, disruption or health impacts. Impacts are major, widespread and/or may last a few days. Orange is uncommon.
Red: very dangerous and possibly life-threatening weather will cause extreme damage and disruption. Impacts are extensive, widespread and prolonged. Red is rare.
Symbols differ by colour: yellow is a circle, orange a diamond, red a triangle, each with an exclamation mark.
The same weather can have different impacts depending on timing, location and population, which is why the colour is tied to impact.
Marine warnings and watches are a separate program (Canadian Marine Warning Program). They do not use colours and keep a single-tier warning system.

Current ECCC definitions: a warning is an urgent message that severe weather is happening or will happen (act now). A watch is issued when conditions are favourable for the development of severe weather (get ready). An advisory is for specific weather events that are less severe but still significant (act now).
Special weather statements are for information only. They are not alerts and are not colour-coded. They flag unusual or inconvenient conditions and add detail beyond usual forecasts.

lesson.h: Alert forms and where they apply (CAP Information Sheet 3, March 2016)

list: In 2016 CAP terms, when an event meets warning criteria forecasters issue a bulletin containing the warning, watch, advisory or statement. Updates and endings generate further messages. (Current ECCC wording says statements are not alerts.)
Audience sectors: public (all warnings and watches), public (all advisories and statements), marine (shorter-duration convective warnings and advisories), aviation (none planned).
Each program within ECCC sets the criteria and update frequency for its warnings.

Alerts issued for selected areas only (jurisdiction of the responsible program): arctic outflow, blowing snow, dust storm, flash freeze, freezing drizzle, frost, snow squall, storm surge, wind (including location-specific wind warnings), plus marine squall and waterspout.
No 'selected areas' note: blizzard, freezing rain, hurricane, rainfall, snowfall, thunderstorm, tornado, tropical storm, weather, winter storm.
In 2013 temperature hazards such as wind chill, heat wave and high humidity were consolidated into two alerts: extreme cold and heat. The detail goes in the message text.
Short notes written by ECCC meteorologists that add context to weather forecasts: possible impacts, an early heads-up on severe weather, or information for people attending outdoor events.
Issued any time meteorologists think extra context will improve public understanding of the forecast and its potential impacts.
Valid time is shown at the top: from one hour up to one week. 'Now' means it is happening now and will end later. A future valid time means the conditions will occur between the stated hours.

Found on the weather website (local forecast page, below the forecast icons and above the text forecasts) and in the WeatherCAN app (bottom of the screen, on the Now, Hourly or 7 Day tab matching the valid period).
MetNotes do not trigger a notification. They are not warnings, only additional information related to the forecast.
They are posted only for a specified period and disappear when it ends.

ECCC now issues severe thunderstorm and tornado warnings to only the area most likely to see the highest impacts, outlined by a shape called a polygon. The goal is to reduce alert fatigue and cut the number of phone alerts. It took effect Tuesday 11 August 2026, with an official launch on Wednesday 12 August (Canadian Press, ECCC backgrounder).
As a storm moves, forecasters can reshape, split or merge the polygon, which triggers notifications along its path. Overlapping warnings for different threats are possible.
Only those two warning types use polygons. Other alerts such as rain and heat, and severe thunderstorm and tornado watches, stay on the broader predetermined alert zones. Rollout is gradual.
Warning text is semi-automated and produced in English and French at the same time.

Alert Ready (TV, radio, wireless) is issued only for tornado warnings and for severe thunderstorm warnings with wind gusts of 130 km/h or more or hail of 7 cm (baseball size) or more. Wireless alerts target recipients by polygon.

WeatherCAN: on Android, notifications only when you or a saved location is inside the polygon. On Apple devices, notifications also when a polygon is within your alert zone even if you are outside; these say 'nearby'.
ECCC shares polygon data and zone data with alerting partners so third-party apps can transition on their own schedules.

Polygon push alerts list locations in nearby areas that could be impacted, ordered by time of arrival, up to 10 locations. They still carry the main hazards (wind, hail, heavy rain) and safety information.
The colour system from November 2025 is unchanged.

lesson.note: Colour is impact plus confidence. A colour on a warning, advisory or watch tells you the level of impact possible in your area.

terms: ECCC description of what a hazard can do at moderate, high and extreme levels. Replaced the former alert criteria.
ECCC chart that combines impact and forecast confidence to choose yellow, orange or red.
Product ECCC may issue instead of an alert for low-impact weather.

Local forecast office rules for each region

questions.e: The colour is found where impact meets confidence on the matrix.

c: High impact with high or very high confidence
Low impact with very high confidence

c: A MetNote or special weather statement

Light frost on exposed surfaces only

Only high-sided vehicles being pushed around

A funnel cloud with no damage at all

Yes: hail 2 cm and gusts 90 km/h
